## Model Comparison and Recommendation

Both models are evaluated on identical held-out test sets across four configurations, shown in @tbl-model-comparison. The SVR had to be fitted on subsamples^[20,000 rows for the grid search, 50,000 for the final train], whereas the NN tuned on reduced subsamples but trained its final model on the full data^[1.1 million rows for community areas at 1h and 6.8 million for census tracts]. Part of the gap between the models therefore reflects how much data each could use, and handling data at this scale is itself an advantage of the network.

| Configuration | SVR R² | NN R² | SVR nMAE | NN nMAE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Community area, 1h | 0.84 | 0.90 | 0.45 | 0.34 |
| Census tract, 1h | 0.63 | 0.87 | 1.95 | 0.42 |
| Community area, 4h | 0.91 | 0.93 | 0.29 | 0.25 |
| Community area, 1d | 0.93 | 0.93 | 0.23 | 0.24 |

: Comparison of SVR and NN across matched spatio-temporal configurations {#tbl-model-comparison}

Each SVR row is its selected variant: community areas at 4h use the log1p target with an RBF kernel, the other three the untransformed target with a polynomial kernel, all with target encoding. The normalized MAE makes the models comparable despite the differing scales of community areas and census tracts.^[Both models are scored on the identical held-out test sets (235,897 rows for community areas at 1h, 1,449,082 for census tracts at 1h, 58,985 at 4h and 9,840 at 1d), so the normalizing denominator is the same for each pair.]

On R² the models converge as the time window widens, tying at 0.93 for 1d and nearly so at 4h (0.91 against 0.93). The difference shows at finer resolutions: at 1h the SVR reaches 0.84 for community areas against 0.90, and it falls to 0.63 for census tracts while the network holds 0.87, most likely because of the additional zeros introduced by the privacy issue. The normalized MAE tells the same story. The network has the lower error at every resolution except the daily one, where the two are effectively tied (0.24 against 0.23). The largest gap is again on census tracts, where the SVR error exceeds mean demand (1.95) against 0.42 for the network.

Neither model is simpler to build. The SVR needed target encoding, log1p, and a custom scorer. The NN replaces the first with embeddings and avoids the other two through an L1 loss robust to the skewed target, but requires architecture and learning-rate search instead. Explicit regularization proved unnecessary, since the search selected zero dropout and zero weight decay for all four final models, leaving early stopping as the only control on overfitting. Only scale separates them: the SVR cannot use the full dataset, which costs it most at the finer resolutions where extra data matters.

Measured against the historical-average rule of thumb from @sec-demand-prediction (nMAE 0.31), the SVR improves only marginally (0.29, a 5.7 percent reduction), most likely because it sees a fraction of the training data, while the network reaches 0.25, roughly 18 percent. The modelling effort barely pays off for the SVR but is substantial for the network, which is the model we would put into production. In practical terms it predicts demand within five trips of the actual count in roughly 83% of all 4h test windows (see @tbl-nn-accuracy).

That leaves the resolution. We recommend community areas in four-hour windows (R² 0.93, nMAE 0.25). Daily forecasts are marginally better on nMAE and marginally worse on R² (0.93, nMAE 0.24), but a daily total is too coarse for a fleet operator to act on, while hourly forecasts add noise without planning value. Census tracts were rejected despite their finer detail, as fewer than half of the records carry usable tract information. That gap carries into predictions learned from reduced counts, which therefore forecast systematically fewer trips than occur because the test set is reduced the same way. The measured error stays low and conceals the bias, but would be clearly visible in production and worst in the low-trip-count areas. Community areas are small enough to act on as the average one covers roughly three square miles,^[Chicago comprises 77 community areas across roughly 227 square miles (U.S. Census Bureau).] which a taxi can cross in under fifteen minutes.
